author: reek
body: The mouse cursor is drawn by saving the pixels beneath it, painting a small white block with a dark border, and restoring the patch on the next move -- a full-panel repaint per mouse twitch would run at report rate for nothing. Any draw that clears or repaints beneath the cursor invalidates the saved patch; the next movement repaints the cursor over the fresh screen. State block: [0] valid, [4] x, [8] y, [12] clamped width, [16] clamped height, saved pixels from [32] at a fixed 16-pixel pitch.

author: reek
body: Hide before a repaint, not just clear the flag: clearing alone is correct only when the repaint covers the cursor. A pane that covers part of the panel leaves the old cursor pixels standing outside it, and the next save-under bakes them into the patch -- a permanent ghost the first restore stamps back. Restore first, then clear; the repaint may then paint anywhere, and the next update saves a clean patch.

author: reek
body: Truncating at `stride` rather than at a visible width is deliberate: the padded region beyond the visible pixels is invisible but harmless, while the next scanline is not. Losing the tail of a long line is a failure the reader can SEE; overwriting the line above it is one they cannot.

author: val
body: The GOP framebuffer is linear 32-bit XRGB; base and stride (pixels per scan line) come from the boot stub's handoff cells. It is ordinary RAM at GPA 0xBF000000 with no MMIO trap, so a read-back costs an ordinary load, which is what makes partial coverage affordable. CBF glyphs are 8x16 and each on-pixel is drawn as a scale-by-scale square.

author: val
body: `(y * stride + x) * 4` has no edge: an `x` past the scan line is the next row and a negative `x` the row above, so a window hanging off the right edge drew its strip down the left of the screen. The READ needs the same bound as the write: dragging a window off the left edge faulted the guest in `peek-32` with `!EXC=0e`, CR2 past 4 GiB, a negative `x` carried into the address as an unsigned 32-bit word. Off the glass answers 0.

author: val
body: Inverts the low 24 bits and leaves the top byte alone: the outline shows over any colour, and the GOP's padding byte is untouched. XOR is its own eraser, so drawing the same frame twice restores every pixel.

author: val
body: The side bands are inset by the thickness so each corner is inverted ONCE; inverting it twice would restore it and notch all four corners.
